newsitem.title: UK: UK SFO calls for action as investor frauds spread.
newsitem.headline: UK SFO calls for action as investor frauds spread.

text.p: Frauds against investors are spreading and Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) said on Monday it wanted tougher action against the perpetrators, including harsh fines.
Rosalind Wright, who took over as director of the SFO earlier this year, is expected to argue for tougher action against fraudsters on the day the SFO publishes its ninth annual report.
"She believes offenders should be hit hard where it hurts them most - in their pockets," SFO spokesman James O'Donoghue said.
This could involve punitive fines and disqualifying fraudsters from any activity involving soliciting or managing the public's investments.
Wright, the fourth director of the SFO, is expected to call on judges to take a harder look at assets held by a defendant's family when assessing their ability to pay.
The SFO, which was set up in 1988 to investigate and prosecute major financial fraud, is probing 42 suspected frauds on investors, up from 29 a year ago.

It is expected to warn people to exercise great vigilance, pointing out that at times of relative economic buoyancy, fraudsters are on the look out for investors seeking new channels for their savings.
Its message will be "don't part with money before taking independent, reliable professional advice".
Novel or unusual investments need to be treated with extra caution as many are likely to fall outside the regulated markets, meaning investors would not be able to claim any compensation.
During the last financial year the SFO worked on the investigation or prosecution of 103 cases. At the end of year, 82 cases were either under investigation or before the courts.
Over the period eight trials were concluded resulting in the conviction of 12 out of 14 defendants. Two defendants were acquitted and in every trial at least one defendant was convicted.
To date the SFO has taken on 158 cases, involving 366 defendants, which have led to 234 convictions.
But this conviction rate of around 64 percent has often been overshadowed by high profile failures to achieve convictions by the SFO.
Wright is unlikely to mount a defence of the SFO's record, but to argue for ways of improving the system, including greater flexibility in the prosecution and trial of serious and complex fraud.

There have been widespread calls for a change to the jury system in such long and complicated trials, which often go on for months. The SFO will argue that more intense efforts on cutting the number of charges and concentrating on key defendants will mean shorter and more focused trials.
